item.title: My simple fix for the messed up Sunday Shows
item.description: The author finds Sunday talk shows frustrating due to their format, repetitive political guests, and focus on Washington D.C. Their simple fix involves changing the format to feature one non-politician guest for a one-on-one interview followed by a round table discussion with experts, eliminating politicians. The author suggests moving the show's location out of Washington D.C. to reflect the country better and broadcasting it throughout the week on various platforms to reach a wider audience. These changes aim to make the shows more engaging and informative by focusing on issues rather than political maneuvering.

item.title: How to Know If You Are Behaving Ethically as a Journalist: Jay Rosen’s Checklist
item.description: Jay Rosen's checklist offers a framework for ethical journalism, focusing on the impact of actions rather than perfect moral behavior. The checklist, developed for students and newsrooms, comprises eight key components: transparency regarding methods and motives; admitting and correcting mistakes; involving the community in newsgathering; showing empathy and humanity towards subjects; actively listening to audiences and sources; ensuring fairness and proportionality in reporting; practicing humility and self-doubt; and demonstrating courage. These principles aim to guide journalists in adapting their ethical practices amidst changes in the field, encouraging accountability and a rational, transparent approach to reporting.

item.title: Why I Don’t Trust a Thing the Church of the Savvy Says About Candidate Obama’s Call for Transparency
item.description: The author reflects on a conversation about Obama's call for transparency and expresses skepticism about its feasibility given the political system's reliance on secrecy. They are concerned that the same people who initially praised Obama's transparency call are now defending the White House's spin tactics, questioning the Church of the Savvy's stance on the issue. The author believes that prioritizing the perceived greater good can erode transparency over time, making them distrustful of any statements made on the topic by this group.

item.title: What I Told the Man from Politics Daily
item.description: The Republican Party in Texas faces internal challenges, despite its history of electoral success. The party struggles with a primary problem, as run-offs often push the party toward extremes, silencing moderate voices. Moderate Republicans sometimes vote in the Democratic primary. However, the party's conservative principles, like low taxes and regulations, remain popular, and the state's growing population brings in new conservative voters. The Republican Party can succeed in Texas by addressing the primary issues and re-integrating moderate viewpoints. The future of the party in Texas is promising, but requires effort.

item.title: Is "He Said, She Said, We're Clueless" Coverage Dying?
item.description: The author critiques Jay Rosen's optimistic view on the decline of "he said, she said" journalism. While acknowledging that sophisticated journalists recognize the flaws of false balance, the author argues that economic pressures in the media industry, including job cuts and the loss of specialized journalists, make the lazy shortcut of "he said, she said" reporting even more prevalent. The author concludes that the blogosphere's ability to counteract this trend is limited due to the underlying economic realities of the media business.

item.title: PressThink: he said/she said Journalism: Lame Formula in the Land of the Active User
item.description: This article critiques the "he said, she said" style of journalism, arguing that it often fails to assess competing truth claims and instead offers a false sense of balance. The author contends that this approach, while seemingly a quick and easy solution to reporting deadlines and the complexity of verifying information, ultimately hinders truth-telling. The rise of the internet and readily available information sources have made this style of reporting increasingly untenable, as readily available evidence allows for a more nuanced and accurate presentation of facts, moving beyond a simple recitation of opposing viewpoints.

item.title: He Said, She Said Journalism: Lame Formula in the Land of the Active User
item.description: The blogosphere has changed journalism, moving it from a one-way communication system to one where many can speak and listen. The "he said, she said" reporting style, which quotes two sides without deeper analysis, is a weak approach because it often fails to understand the situation or provide genuine balance. This forces readers, the "active users" of the web, to independently evaluate the information and determine the truth, making the reporting style insufficient.

item.title: “He Said/She Said” Journalism: Lame Formula in the Land of the Active User
item.description: The "he said/she said" formula, common in news coverage, often presents conflicting viewpoints without adequate evaluation of their merit. While suitable for reporting negotiations, it can misrepresent issues where consensus exists on one side, such as scientific findings. This approach can be perceived as weak reporting by active online news consumers who are more engaged and critical of news construction. This active audience can see alternative ways for journalists to distinguish between credible and less credible claims, ultimately highlighting the need for journalistic judgment rather than merely presenting opposing arguments.

item.title: PressThink: Introducing the new Huffington Post Investigative Fund (And My Own Role in It)
item.description: The Huffington Post launches the Huffington Post Investigative Fund, a non-profit initiative funded by The Huffington Post and The Atlantic Philanthropies, aimed at producing investigative journalism. Jay Rosen, a senior advisor to the project, discusses its goals, including the use of open-source and distributed reporting methods, collaboration between professional and amateur journalists, and the importance of high verification standards. The Fund aims to 'report once, run anywhere,' making its content freely available for republication. The initiative sparks discussions about the future of investigative journalism, particularly its role in smaller communities.

item.title: Flying Seminar on the Future of News
item.description: This article curates a collection of essays and blog posts from March 2009, forming a 'flying seminar' on the future of news in the face of the newspaper industry's crisis. The pieces explore various perspectives, from the sociological implications of the decline of the traditional press (Paul Starr, Yochai Benkler) to the internal struggles of news organizations (Clay Shirky) and the potential of new media ecosystems (Steven Berlin Johnson). The authors discuss the changing production models of news, the potential for citizen journalism, and the challenges of adapting to a rapidly evolving media landscape.

item.title: PressThink: It Took 23 Years, But I Finally Got to Give My View of the National Press on National Television
item.description: This post reflects on Jay Rosen's appearance on Bill Moyers Journal, discussing his article "Audience Atomization Overcome" and the lack of coverage in the mainstream press. Rosen highlights the discrepancy between the blogosphere's reception and the silence from the established political press, emphasizing his unique perspective gained from years of studying the national press. He expresses gratitude to Bill Moyers, PBS, and Glenn Greenwald for their support.

item.title: Write it yourself
item.description: This article reflects on the relationship between the presidency and the press, tracing its evolution from Theodore Roosevelt's proactive engagement with the media to George W. Bush's strategic distancing. The author argues that Barack Obama's presidency presents an opportunity to redefine this relationship, advocating for greater transparency and a more direct engagement with the public, moving beyond the traditional model of a single interlocutor (the White House press corps) and the dominance of 'Big Media'. The author emphasizes the need for Obama to actively shape the narrative, urging him to 'write it himself' – to control the information flow and actively engage with a broader, more diverse media landscape.

item.title: PressThink: Audience Atomization Overcome: Why the Internet Weakens the Authority of the Press
item.description: This article analyzes Daniel C. Hallin's model of the three spheres of journalism (consensus, legitimate debate, and deviance) to explain how the US political press operates. Hallin's model reveals how journalists implicitly define what constitutes acceptable political discourse, often marginalizing dissenting views and reinforcing existing power structures. The rise of the internet and blogging, however, allows like-minded individuals to connect, challenging the press's ability to control the narrative and define consensus, a phenomenon the author summarizes as “audience atomization overcome.”

item.title: Audience Atomization Overcome: Why the Internet Weakens the Authority of the Press
item.description: The internet weakens the press's authority by fostering a connected public that can discuss, challenge, and create its own narratives about news. This shift from an atomized audience to a connected one diminishes the press's control over opinion formation, the number of witnesses at events, definitions of the news, master narratives, framing, news filters, and professional ideology. The press now faces competition from public discourse and alternative information sources, requiring it to justify its authority and position in the evolving media landscape.

item.title: Audience Atomization Overcome: Why the Internet Weakens the Authority of the Press
item.description: The internet fundamentally alters the authority of the press by dismantling audience atomization. Historically, the audience was isolated, reliant on the press to understand public sentiment and actions. The internet allows for public gatherings, comparison of ideas, the development of collective voices, and public action. This shift diminishes the press's exclusive ability to represent the public. The press retains authority, but must adapt by fostering public discourse, facilitating conversations, and partnering with the public in news production to regain its influence in the new environment.

item.title: Why I Write 400 Words a Day and Put Them on Twitter
item.description: This article documents the author's process of writing a piece about his use of Twitter for the Chronicle of Higher Education. It details his approach to explaining Twitter to a non-Twitter using audience, outlining the key aspects he plans to cover, and soliciting input from his readers on how they utilize the platform. The author frames his Twitter usage as a hand-built tipster network and seeks similar experiences from others to enrich his article.

item.title: PressThink: Make Something Valuable to Journalism and Give it Away: Stanford Re-Deploys its Journalism Fellows
item.description: This article discusses a shift in the Knight Fellowships at Stanford University, moving away from a model of general enrichment for mid-career journalists to one focused on journalistic innovation and entrepreneurship. The change is driven by the instability of the news industry, with newsrooms increasingly unable to absorb returning fellows or value their newly acquired knowledge. The new model emphasizes the creation of tangible, public goods by fellows, mirroring an open-source approach and aiming to increase the fellowship's impact on journalism beyond the individual level.

item.title: If Bloggers Had No Ethics Blogging Would Have Failed, But it Didn’t. So Let’s Get a Clue.
item.description: This article explores the evolving relationship between bloggers and journalists in the early days of the internet. Rosen argues that the distinctions between traditional journalism and blogging are less about inherent ethics and more about the different structures of closed and open editorial systems. He highlights the differences in production methods, gatekeeping versus filtering, and the nature of trust in each system. Ultimately, he contends that the success of blogging demonstrates that it has developed its own ethics based on the trust built between bloggers and their audiences within the open platform.

item.title: PressThink: The Palin Convention and the Culture War Option
item.description: John McCain's selection of Sarah Palin as his running mate is analyzed as a culture war strategy aimed at creating conflict with journalists and bloggers, exploiting the resentment narrative, and focusing on personalities rather than issues. The strategy hinges on Palin's charisma and the ensuing controversy, leveraging both the intense support from social conservatives and the negative press coverage to generate a wave of attention and fundraising. The author notes the risks involved and the uncertainty of the strategy's success.

item.title: PressThink: Hype Busting at Mother Jones Goes Bust
item.description: This article critiques a Mother Jones feature questioning whether Barack Obama's campaign rhetoric exaggerated its historical significance. The author challenges the feature's premise, arguing that there's no direct quote or evidence supporting the claim that Obama compared his campaign to past progressive movements. The author details their correspondence with Mother Jones editors, revealing a missing contextual speech excerpt that partially justifies the feature's framing, but still leaves crucial aspects unaddressed. The article highlights the dangers of inadvertently creating hype while attempting to debunk it and questions the journalistic rigor of the Mother Jones piece.

item.title: National Explainer
item.description: This article analyzes the success of "The Giant Pool of Money," a This American Life episode explaining the mortgage crisis. Rosen argues that the episode's effectiveness stems from its prioritizing of explanation over simply reporting facts. He contends that traditional journalism often fails to provide the necessary background context for understanding complex news events, leading to audience disengagement. He proposes a shift in journalistic priorities, advocating for the creation of more explanatory pieces that serve as prerequisites for understanding subsequent news reports, thereby increasing audience engagement and comprehension.

item.title: "The Whole Anthrax Case Would Make For a Good Journalism Class." Brian Ross Responds.
item.description: This article analyzes Brian Ross's response to questions regarding ABC News's inaccurate anthrax reporting in 2001. The author presents a fictional Q&A summarizing Ross's responses, highlighting inconsistencies and raising concerns about the network's handling of the situation, lack of corrections, and potential implications for the relationship between media, government, and the public. The piece also discusses the broader implications of the incident for journalism and its relationship with power in the post-Iraq War era.

item.title: Three Vital Questions for ABC News About its Anthrax Reporting in 2001
item.description: This article details a coordinated effort by bloggers and journalists to hold ABC News accountable for its 2001 anthrax reporting, which falsely linked Iraqi involvement. The author, Jay Rosen, and Dan Gillmor posed three key questions to ABC News regarding the sourcing and accuracy of their reporting, emphasizing the importance of transparency and accountability when confidential sources mislead. The response from ABC News, along with commentary from various journalists and publications, highlighted the ethical dilemmas surrounding confidential sources and the need for investigative journalism to correct the record in cases of significant misinformation.

item.title: A Most Useful Definition
item.description: This article explores the definition of citizen journalism, focusing on the author's concise definition: "When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism." The author discusses various perspectives on the term, including those from bloggers and other media analysts, and highlights the implications for the traditional news media, suggesting that citizen journalism represents a shift in how information is created and disseminated, moving away from a model of the press as a singular information pipeline.

item.title: PressThink: Big Daddy Newspaper Has Gone and Left Journalism
item.description: This article contrasts two responses to the decline of traditional newspapers. One is the curmudgeonly resistance of veteran journalists clinging to the past, exemplified by the hostile reactions to a young intern's positive assessment of her editor's restructuring plans. The other is a proactive approach, represented by the Tree House Media Project, which empowers journalists to become self-publishers and adapt to the changing media landscape. Rosen argues that the future lies in embracing self-reliance and abandoning the 'mass' identity of traditional media in favor of more human-scale approaches.

item.title: PressThink: Migration Point for the Press Tribe
item.description: This 2008 essay by Jay Rosen uses the metaphor of migration to describe the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that professional journalists, facing the decline of their traditional business model, must adapt to a new media landscape characterized by two-way communication, horizontal sharing, and the rise of citizen journalism. He highlights the challenges of this transition, including resistance from within the profession and the need to integrate professional and amateur journalism practices. Rosen uses the example of OffTheBus, a project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington, as an illustration of a distributed reporting model for campaign coverage.

item.title: Update on Beatblogging.org Six Months In
item.description: This post updates the progress of Beatblogging.org, a project exploring whether beat reporters can improve their work by using social networks. David Cohn, the original editor, has secured funding for a new project, spot.us, and Patrick Thornton has taken over Beatblogging.org. The project will continue to profile beat reporters using networked approaches and collaborate with WiredJournalists.com to reach a wider audience of innovative journalists.

item.title: The McCain News Hunt
item.description: This article details a collaborative project, the "McCain News Hunt," which utilized NewsTrust, a platform for rating and sharing news stories, and OffTheBus to crowdsource the best journalism about John McCain during a specific week. Participants rated 233 stories, resulting in a ranked list highlighting the top-rated pieces and demonstrating the potential of social media and collaborative filtering to improve news discovery and quality in a proliferating media landscape.

item.title: PressThink: When Mayhill Fowler Met Bill Clinton at the Rope Line
item.description: This article analyzes a case involving Mayhill Fowler, a citizen journalist contributing to OffTheBus, who obtained an off-the-record comment from Bill Clinton. The incident sparks a debate about the ethics and implications of citizen journalism, particularly concerning transparency, the changing nature of 'off the record' interactions, and the relationship between professional and citizen journalists. The author explores the evolving media landscape and questions traditional journalistic practices in light of the increased accessibility of information and the blurring lines between professional and amateur reporting.

item.title: PressThink: The Jerk at the Podium: Scott McClellan Steps Away
item.description: This article analyzes Scott McClellan's tenure as White House press secretary, arguing that his role was not to communicate effectively but to actively frustrate and delegitimize the press. McClellan's ineffectiveness, far from being accidental, was a deliberate strategy – part of a broader 'Rollback' policy to diminish the press's influence and enhance executive power. This involved minimizing communication, refusing detailed answers, and promoting an environment of non-engagement to reduce the press's ability to hold the administration accountable.

item.title: PressThink: What Happened to Scott McClellan in Longer Perspective: 100 Years of the White House Press
item.description: This article analyzes Scott McClellan's post-White House reflections, connecting his experience as press secretary to a broader shift in White House communication strategies under the Bush administration. Rosen argues that the Bush administration strategically employed non-communication and opacity, rejecting the traditional role of the press as an interlocutor between the presidency and the public. This departure from the Roosevelt-era model, where the president actively engaged with the press, represented a calculated effort to enhance executive power by controlling information flow and avoiding accountability. McClellan's regret and public acknowledgment of his role in this strategy highlight the consequences of this approach and its ultimate failure in maintaining public support.

item.title: Looking for the Mouse in Media: Clay Shirky on Deploying the Cognitive Surplus for Public Good
item.description: This article discusses Clay Shirky's concept of "cognitive surplus," the vast amount of free time previously consumed by television, and its potential for productive online activity. Rosen uses Shirky's ideas to explore the shift from passive media consumption to active participation and creation, exemplified by his daughter's blogging activities. He contrasts the passive nature of traditional media with the interactive possibilities of the web, highlighting the need for new media projects to utilize this untapped potential for social good.

item.title: PressThink: The Presses Stop But the Press Goes On: Capital Times Lives on the Web
item.description: This article details the transformation of the Capital Times, a Madison, Wisconsin newspaper, from a daily print publication to a primarily online news outlet with two weekly print editions. The shift, driven by economic pressures and the changing media landscape, involves job losses, a move to a digital-first strategy, and a re-evaluation of the paper's role in the community. The author analyzes the challenges and potential opportunities presented by this transition, considering the competitive online environment and the paper's legacy as a progressive voice in Madison.

item.title: Newspapers and the Net: Where’s the Business Model, People?
item.description: This article explores the crisis facing newspapers due to the internet's disruption of their traditional business models. Rosen discusses the challenges of transitioning from an advertising-subsidized model to sustainable alternatives, questioning whether the public good of quality journalism can be maintained. He examines various approaches, including non-profit models like ProPublica, innovative ventures like The Politico, and the potential for filtering and repackaging online content. The article also touches upon the inherent inefficiencies of advertising and the need for increased public understanding of the true cost of serious journalism.

item.title: Mayhill Fowler and the Uncharted Territory of Citizen Journalism
item.description: This article discusses the case of Mayhill Fowler, an Obama supporter and citizen journalist who reported on comments made by Obama at a fundraiser. Her report, published on the Huffington Post's OffTheBus blog, was picked up by major news outlets but was subsequently downplayed by Meet the Press, leading to a discussion about the evolving role of citizen journalism in political coverage and the challenges faced by traditional media in navigating this new landscape. The article explores the blurred lines between citizen journalist, campaign supporter, and news reporter, highlighting the lack of established frameworks for understanding this emerging phenomenon.

item.title: PressThink: The Love Affair Between McCain and the Press Sprains the Brain of the Liberal Blogosphere
item.description: This article analyzes the emerging conflict between liberal bloggers and mainstream media regarding their coverage of John McCain's presidential campaign in 2008. The author questions whether a declared 'blogospheric war' against the media is truly underway, or if the situation is more nuanced and dynamic. The piece examines the media's perceived favoritism towards McCain, the bloggers' strategies to counter this narrative, and the potential impact of McCain's unprecedented openness to press questioning on the campaign.

item.title: The News about the news: Jay Rosen
item.description: The program features a discussion with media critic and NYU professor Jay Rosen about the current state of news and its role in a divided America. It highlights the business aspects of news in the digital age, while also acknowledging its importance as a public good. The conversation centers on the challenges facing journalism, including shrinking newsrooms, rising disinformation, and declining trust. Rosen advocates for a shift in journalistic approach, urging the press to move beyond objectivity and neutrality to actively defend democracy by calling out misinformation and supporting democratic norms. The discussion also includes the impact of AI on journalism, the future of local news, and the challenge of rebuilding public trust.

item.title: PressThink: Just How Did John McCain Obtain What He Has in the Bank with the Press?
item.description: This article analyzes the unusually positive relationship between John McCain's presidential campaign and the press corps. The author argues that McCain's willingness to engage in extensive, off-the-record conversations with reporters, even when facing tough questions, cultivated a sense of rapport and trust, creating a 'reputational capital' that shielded him from harsher criticism. The author contrasts this with other candidates' more guarded approaches, highlighting how McCain's openness, while potentially containing strategic elements, inadvertently humanized both him and the reporters, resulting in more favorable coverage. The article also explores whether Barack Obama should adopt a similar strategy.

item.title: PressThink: Obama tells the Best Political Team on Television: You Have a Choice
item.description: This post critiques CNN's Wolf Blitzer's analysis of Barack Obama's speech addressing the Jeremiah Wright controversy. Rosen argues that Blitzer's interpretation, focusing solely on political strategy, misses the speech's deeper message urging a transcendence of divisive political discourse and a more nuanced understanding of race. Rosen contrasts Blitzer's shallow analysis with the insightful observations of Greg Sargent and Charles Murray, highlighting Obama's direct challenge to the media's role in perpetuating a spectacle-driven, race-focused narrative.

item.title: Pincus, Neutrality, and the Politics of News
item.description: This article critiques the prevailing notion of journalistic neutrality, arguing that it hinders effective political reporting and undermines democratic processes. It uses examples like Clark Hoyt's defense of the New York Times' neutrality, Josh Marshall's TPM's transparently liberal approach, and Walter Pincus' call for journalistic courage to illustrate the need for a more politically engaged and self-aware press. The piece emphasizes the importance of fairness over neutrality, advocating for transparency about reporters' political affiliations and a reevaluation of the power dynamics between the press and government, particularly addressing the legacy of controlled messaging started during the Reagan administration.

item.title: PressThink: "An Attractively Against-the-Grain Enterprise..."
item.description: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, engage in 'misguided contrarianism' by publishing provocative or seemingly iconoclastic pieces that ultimately serve to promote the paper's self-image rather than contribute meaningfully to public discourse. It critiques the pressure to 'find something' on all political candidates and the tendency to prioritize staff morale or economic concerns over journalistic integrity.

item.title: Three Stories That Went Awry
item.description: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, publish controversial or seemingly contrarian pieces, suggesting that these actions are often driven by a desire to shape the publication's self-image as independent and iconoclastic rather than a genuine pursuit of truth or impactful journalism. The author critiques this 'misguided contrarianism,' arguing that it can lead to poor editorial decisions and a misreading of cultural politics.

item.title: PressThink: Three Vetting Stories Went Awry at the New York Times: Find the Pattern.
item.description: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decisions to investigate Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He argues that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks Romenesko readers for insights into what might have been the common factors behind these editorial choices during the vetting process of presidential candidates.

item.title: PressThink: Three Vetting Stories Went Awry at the New York Times: Find the Pattern.
item.description: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decision-making process in pursuing stories about Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He notes that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks for insights into what might be the common thread among these cases of questionable journalistic judgment.

item.title: Cliff Notes Ver.
item.description: This article is a distillation of a New York Times Q&A with readers regarding their explosive report on John McCain's involvement with lobbyist Vicki Iseman. The NYT defends its reporting choices, addressing concerns about anonymity, the inclusion of potentially unverified information about a romantic relationship, the timing of the story, and the potential impact on McCain's campaign. They maintain the story's accuracy and their commitment to thorough investigative journalism, despite the significant backlash.

item.title: PressThink: Public Editor to Bill Keller: "You Haven't Got it."
item.description: This article analyzes the New York Times' handling of a story suggesting John McCain had an affair. The author criticizes the Times' editors for lacking political awareness, failing to understand the potential consequences of their reporting, and clinging to journalistic codes that prevented them from recognizing the political realities of the situation. He argues that the Times' readers exhibited a more nuanced understanding of the political implications than the editors, highlighting a credibility gap between the newspaper and its audience.

item.title: For the New York Times, Too, Self-Confidence on Ethics Poses Risks
item.description: This blog post analyzes the New York Times's reporting on John McCain's alleged affair, questioning the timing of the story in relation to the paper's endorsement of McCain. The author raises concerns about the reliance on anonymous sources, the potential impact on the 2008 election, and the broader implications for media ethics and the relationship between the newsroom and editorial page. The piece also highlights the ensuing culture war and the Times's discomfort with defending its journalistic choices in the court of public opinion.

item.title: The Beast Without a Brain: Why Horse Race Journalism Works for Journalists and Fails Us
item.description: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the campaign media operates as a 'herd of independent minds' lacking a central direction or capacity to learn from mistakes. This mindlessness results in superficial coverage focused on predicting outcomes rather than understanding the stakes, leading to inaccurate narratives and a failure to inform the public effectively.

item.title: The Beast Without a Brain: Why Horse Race Journalism Works for Journalists and Fails Us
item.description: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the media's focus on predicting outcomes and insider perspectives results in a "herd of independent minds" incapable of critical thinking or adapting to new information. He contends that this mindlessness leads to inaccurate and uninformative reporting, as journalists prioritize conventional routines over genuine insight and analysis.

item.title: PressThink: "Most of them are not ideologically driven; they just want to get on the front page."
item.description: This article analyzes the contrasting views of the conservative elite and the conservative base regarding the media. While the base often perceives the press as monolithic, liberal, and against the Bush administration, key figures like Karl Rove and Dan Bartlett, having gained insider experience, recognize a more nuanced reality. They acknowledge the press's inherent desire for compelling stories and its oppositional stance towards power, irrespective of party affiliation. This divergence highlights a strategic utilization of the base's perception of media bias to serve political goals, while insiders operate with a more pragmatic understanding of journalistic motivations.
